core: The working definition of a firewall: a system that filters traffic between networks based on rules (NIST SP 800-41: a device or program that controls the flow of network traffic between networks or hosts that employ differing security postures)
The gatekeeper analogy: a firewall decides what crosses the boundary between a trusted and an untrusted network, in both directions
How filtering works conceptually: rules about what is allowed in and out, based on addresses, ports, and types of traffic — no configuration how-to
Hardware/network firewalls vs software/host-based firewalls: the device at the network edge vs the program on a single device
Default deny vs default allow: the two philosophies, and why default deny is the more secure posture (NIST recommendation)
Firewall limits, honestly framed: encrypted and tunneled traffic, insider threats, and social engineering are not stopped by a firewall alone
supporting: Firewall policy as the expression of what an organization needs: which addresses, ports, protocols, and applications may cross the boundary (NIST SP 800-41)
Host-based and personal firewalls as an additional layer protecting individual devices, including laptops off the office network (NIST SP 800-41)
Firewalls can only work effectively on traffic they can inspect; cryptography and tunneling hide traffic from inspection (NIST SP 800-41)
Social engineering attacks manipulate people rather than technical controls, so they bypass firewalls (CISA)
outOfScope: Network fundamentals — addressing, ports, protocols, routing in detail (sibling topic: cybersecurity:foundations:network-fundamentals; referenced only)
Network segmentation — DMZs, zones, internal segmentation (sibling topic: cybersecurity:foundations:network-segmentation)
Wi-Fi security — wireless encryption and home router hardening (sibling topic: cybersecurity:foundations:wi-fi-security)

Firewall configuration, rule syntax, or product-specific setup (literacy level: no config how-to)
Attack techniques, exploit details, or offensive methods (defensive framing only)

claims.claim: A firewall is a device or program that controls the flow of network traffic between networks or hosts that employ differing security postures; in plain terms, a system that filters traffic between networks based on rules.

Cloudflare defines a firewall as a security system that monitors and controls network traffic based on a set of security rules, and notes that firewalls usually sit between a trusted network and an untrusted network — often the Internet.

A firewall policy defines how firewalls handle inbound and outbound network traffic for specific IP addresses and address ranges, protocols, applications, and content types; rules can therefore be based on addresses, ports, and types of traffic, and firewalls filter traffic in both directions.

Deny by default means blocking all inbound and outbound traffic that has not been expressly permitted by firewall policy; NIST states that deny by default is a more secure approach than permitting all traffic that is not explicitly forbidden, and recommends blocking all traffic not expressly permitted because such traffic is not needed.

Firewalls come in two broad forms: network firewalls — devices placed at the perimeter of a network with external and internal interfaces that filter traffic for the networks behind them — and host-based (personal) firewalls — software on a single host that monitors and controls that host's own incoming and outgoing traffic.
Firewalls were originally hardware appliances, while many modern firewalls are software-based and can run on several different types of hardware (Cloudflare).

A firewall can only work effectively on traffic that it can inspect: encrypted traffic (such as TLS, IPsec, SSH, and encrypted email or files) hides its contents from the firewall, tunneled traffic may be unintelligible to it, and network firewalls cannot recognize all instances and forms of attack.

Insider threats are a firewall limit: attacks sent from one internal host to another often do not pass through the network firewall, and an attacker who compromises a host and gains administrator-level privileges can disable or circumvent a host-based firewall.

Social engineering is a firewall limit: such attacks manipulate people rather than technical controls, so they do not depend on crossing the firewall; CISA's guidance treats verifying requests through another channel as the defense against them.

conflictingEvidence.issue: Firewalls are sometimes described as a complete perimeter wall and sometimes as one layer among several.
positions: Marketing-style framing: a firewall is a wall that blocks attacks at the network edge.

NIST SP 800-41: network firewalls cannot recognize all instances and forms of attack, attacks between internal hosts often do not pass through the network firewall, and firewall functionality is now often added beyond the perimeter as one layer of security.
Cloudflare: firewalls can intercept malicious traffic before it reaches the network and prevent sensitive information from leaving, but are one of several network security technologies.
conflictingEvidence.resolution: The lesson presents the firewall as a boundary gatekeeper that is one layer of defense, not a complete wall; the limits section makes the honest framing explicit.

conflictingEvidence.issue: Default deny is the recommended posture, but organizations do not always block all outbound traffic.
positions: NIST SP 800-41 recommends that all inbound and outbound traffic not expressly permitted should be blocked (deny by default).

The same document notes that less stringent policies are generally used for outgoing traffic because organizations permit users to reach a wide range of external applications on millions of external hosts.
conflictingEvidence.resolution: The lesson teaches default deny as the more secure philosophy and the recommended starting point, while noting that outbound rules are often deliberately more permissive because users need many external services.
